title: Feedback That Clicks: Introductory Physics Students’ Valued Features in AI Feedback Generated From Self-Crafted and Engineered Prompts
extended_summary:
This paper examines how introductory physics students use generative AI to obtain feedback on their physics arguments, and what kinds of AI-generated feedback they find most useful. The authors focus on three questions: how sophisticated students’ self-written prompts are when asking AI for feedback, what features students value in AI feedback, and whether students prefer feedback produced from their own prompts or from more structured prompts that incorporate prompt-engineering techniques and principles of effective feedback.

The study was conducted as an extra-credit assignment in a large-enrollment calculus-based introductory physics course for future engineers at Purdue University in Spring 2025. Students completed a physics task about the physical meaning of the slope of a gravitational potential energy versus distance graph, then used an AI platform of their choice to request feedback on their Claim-Evidence-Reasoning argument in three ways: with a self-crafted prompt, with a provided prompt using foundational prompt-engineering techniques, and with a provided prompt that combined prompt-engineering with educational principles of effective feedback. The dataset included 1,235 qualified responses from 1,661 respondents out of 2,044 enrolled students. The analysis combined quantitative coding of prompt features and rankings with qualitative emergent coding of students’ written justifications.

The authors found that students’ self-crafted prompts usually included only a subset of foundational prompting techniques, and none combined all four focal techniques analyzed. Even when prompts were incomplete or ambiguous, AI often inferred the intended task context correctly, though the resulting feedback was not always conceptually accurate or fully appropriate. From students’ justifications, the authors identified 12 valued feedback features grouped into four themes: Evaluation, Content, Presentation, and Depth. Students especially valued feedback that critiqued their work, highlighted strengths, offered actionable guidance, and presented information clearly and concisely.

Overall, students strongly preferred feedback generated from structured prompts, especially prompts that combined prompt engineering with principles of effective feedback. Feedback from self-crafted prompts was most often ranked least useful. The paper concludes that AI feedback systems in STEM education should be designed not only with prompt-engineering strategies but also with established principles of effective feedback, and that prompt engineering itself may be an important skill to teach in introductory physics courses.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot used to generate natural-language feedback on student work from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Introductory physics students used AI platforms of their choice to obtain feedback on CER-style arguments about the physical meaning of the slope of a gravitational potential energy vs. distance graph. The study compared feedback generated from self-crafted prompts versus provided structured prompts incorporating prompt engineering and effective-feedback principles.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative/mixed-methods study of introductory physics students, 90.2% of student-crafted prompts explicitly requested feedback, 61.8% evidenced both clear task context and explicit inclusion of the student’s argument, and none included all four foundational prompt-engineering techniques together. Among 293 prompts lacking clear or complete context descriptions, AI correctly interpreted the context in 285 cases (97%), but the paper notes that responses were not always fully appropriate or conceptually correct.
findings.measure: Prompt sophistication and AI contextual interpretation of physics-feedback prompts
findings.sample_size: n=1151 prompts for prompt analysis; 293 ambiguous/incomplete-context cases

findings.finding_summary: Students overwhelmingly preferred feedback generated from structured prompts over feedback generated from their own self-crafted prompts. Of 1235 responses, 61.4% ranked feedback from prompts combining prompt engineering with effective-feedback principles (Feedback C) as most useful, 29.7% ranked prompt-engineering-only feedback (Feedback B) first, and only 8.9% ranked self-crafted-prompt feedback (Feedback A) first; 91.1% thus preferred one of the structured-prompt conditions as their top choice.
findings.measure: Student ranking of perceived usefulness of AI-generated feedback across prompt types

findings.finding_summary: From 1160 valid student justifications, the most frequently valued AI-feedback features fell under Evaluation (69.4%), followed by Content (55.2%), Presentation (47.8%), and Depth (44.2%). Students preferring the prompt that combined prompt engineering and effective-feedback principles most often emphasized critique (48.4%), guidance (52.4%), conciseness (36.2%), and specificity (27.7%), indicating preference for feedback that clearly identifies weaknesses and offers actionable next steps.
findings.measure: Student-perceived useful features of AI-generated feedback

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical course-based study with large samples, but the reported evidence is primarily descriptive and qualitative/mixed-methods rather than an RCT or strong quasi-experimental design estimating causal effects on learning outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear positive student preferences for structured AI feedback, but it does not report standardized effect sizes or direct causal gains in achievement, so overall impact magnitude remains unclear.
